book.title: The Weight of a Small Town
book.author: Tobi Adeyemi

lines: In Okwe, everybody knew what you carried before you did.
The baker knew your mother's cough.
The mechanic knew your father's debts.
And Mrs. Ibe, who sold phone credit under a faded umbrella at the junction, knew when you were in love, usually a week before you admitted it to yourself.
I left at nineteen with one bag and a confidence I had not earned.
Nobody knew my name or my mother's cough or whether I had eaten.
For eleven years I called that freedom.
Then my father died, and I came back on a bus that smelled of onions and rain, and the first person I saw at the junction was Mrs. Ibe.
She did not say she was sorry.
She pressed a small cold bottle of Fanta into my hand, the way she had when I was seven, and said, "You are thinner."
I cried there, in front of everyone, over a bottle of orange soda, and no one looked away.
That is the weight of a small town.
It is heavy only until you are tired enough to set something down, and find forty pairs of hands already open.
